chunks: What al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated, from Fadala, from al-Husayn, from Ibn Muskan, from 'Umar ibn Hanzala:

He said: I said to Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him): 'May I be made your ransom! I asked you about making up (qada') the daytime salat at night while traveling, and you said: Do not make it up. And our companions asked you, and you said: Make them up.' He said to me: 'Shall I then tell them: Do not pray? For I am reluctant to tell them: Do not pray. By God, that [obligation] is not upon them.'

The other interpretation is that both reports were directed at one who had missed the nawafil salat while in residence (hadar), such that their time had entered upon him before he departed and he had not performed them — so it was incumbent upon him to make them up thereafter. [A subsequent narration] indicates this.

key_terms.النَّوَافِلِ: nawafil — voluntary/supererogatory prayers beyond the obligatory
key_terms.الْحَضَرِ: hadar — state of residence, as opposed to travel (safar)
key_terms.الْوَجْهُ الْآخَرُ: al-wajh al-akhar — the other interpretive angle; al-Tusi's jurisprudential reconciliation
key_terms.قَضَاءِ: qada' — making up missed prayers after their time has elapsed

ai.seo_question: Is it obligatory to make up missed supererogatory prayers (nawafil) when traveling, according to Imam al-Sadiq (AS) in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration presents 'Umar ibn Hanzala's account of receiving apparently contradictory rulings from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) regarding qada' of nawafil prayers missed during daytime travel. The Imam clarifies that telling people 'do not pray' is not what He intends; the obligation is simply not binding upon them. Shaykh al-Tusi then offers a jurisprudential reconciliation: both reports may have addressed a person whose prayer times entered while still in residence before departure, making qada' incumbent.
